en: Vibhaṅga:
Analysis of the Aggregates 1.
Exposition according to the Discourses (Suttantabhājanīya)
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The five aggregates are:
the aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations, and the aggregate of consciousness.
1.1. The Aggregate of Form (Rūpakkhandha).
Therein, what is the aggregate of form?
Whatever form there is—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—all that, having gathered it together and condensed it into one—
This is called the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*).
In this context, what is past form?
That form which is past, ceased, vanished, changed, come to an end, utterly passed away, having arisen [and then perished].

That which has passed away, belongs to the past, and is comprised within the past; namely, the four great elements and the derived matter dependent upon the four great elements—this is called past matter.
In this context, what is future matter?
That form which is unborn, unbecome, unoriginated, unproduced, unmanifested, unarisen, not fully arisen, not established,
not fully established, future, and comprised within the future— namely,
the four great elements and the derived form dependent upon the four great elements.
This is called future form.
In this context, what is present form?
That form which is born, become, fully born, produced, brought forth, manifested, arisen, and fully arisen.
That which has arisen, has fully arisen, is present, and is included within the present— namely,
the four great elements and the derived matter dependent on the four great elements—
this is called present form.
In this context, what is internal form?

That form which, for various beings, is internal, personal, one's own, individual, and clung-to; namely, the four great elements and the derived form based upon the four great elements—this is called internal form.
In this context, what is external form?

Whatever form belongs internally, individually, specifically, and personally to various other beings and other persons, and is clung to— the four great elements and the derived form based on the four great elements—
this is called external form.
In this context, what is gross material form?
The eye-base …pe… the tangible-object-base—
this is called gross material form.
In this context, what is subtle material form?
The female faculty … [and so on] … edible food.
This is called subtle form.
Therein, what is inferior form?

That form which is despised, looked down upon, reviled, despised, and disregarded by this or that being; which is inferior, considered inferior, and regarded as inferior; which is undesirable, unlovely, and disagreeable—namely, forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles.
This is called inferior form.
In this context, what is superior form?

That form which is approved, not disapproved, not despised, not held in contempt, esteemed, considered superior, regarded as superior, desirable, lovely, and pleasing for various beings—namely, forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles.
This is called refined form.
Furthermore, having taken this or that form as a basis, form should be seen as either inferior or refined.
In this context, what is form that is distant?
The faculty of femininity … [and so on] … edible food; or whatever other material form there is that is not near, not close by, distant, and remote—this is called material form that is distant.
In this context, what is material form that is near?
The eye-base …pe… the tangible-object-base, or whatever other material form there is that is near, close by, not distant, in proximity—
this is called material form that is near.
Furthermore, depending on this or that material form, material form should be regarded as either distant or near.
1.2. The Aggregate of Feeling.
Therein, what is the aggregate of feeling?
Whatever feeling there is—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—all that, having gathered it together as one and condensed it—
This is called the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-khandha*).
In this context, what is past feeling?

That feeling which is past, ceased, vanished, changed, come to an end, utterly passed away, having arisen and then vanished; that which is past and comprised within the past: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
This is called past feeling.
In that regard, what is future feeling?
It is that feeling which is unborn, has not come to be, is unarisen, unproduced, not fully produced, not manifested, unarisen, and not fully arisen.
That which has not yet arisen, has not yet emerged, is future, and is comprised within the future— namely, pleasant feeling, painful feeling,
and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling:
this is called future feeling.
In this context, what is present feeling?
That feeling which is born, become, fully arisen, produced, fully manifested, appeared, arisen, fully arisen, emerged, fully emerged, present,
and included within the category of the present— that is, pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
This is called present feeling.
Therein, what is internal feeling?
Whatever feeling is internal, personal, one's own, individual, and clung-to by various beings—whether pleasant feeling, painful feeling, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
This is called internal feeling.
In this context, what is external feeling?

Whatever feeling belongs to various other beings, other persons—internal, individual, personal, and appropriated—whether it be pleasant feeling, painful feeling, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
This is called feeling that is external.
In this context, what is feeling that is gross and what is subtle?
Unwholesome feeling is gross; wholesome and indeterminate feeling is subtle.
Wholesome and unwholesome feelings are gross; indeterminate feelings are subtle.
Painful feeling is gross; pleasant and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings are subtle.
Pleasant and painful feelings are gross; neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is subtle.
The feeling of one who has not attained meditative absorption is gross; the feeling of one who has attained meditative absorption is subtle.
Feeling associated with taints is gross; feeling free from taints is subtle.
Furthermore, feeling should be regarded as gross or subtle in relation to this or that particular feeling.
In this context, what is feeling that is inferior and what is superior?
Unwholesome feeling is inferior; wholesome and indeterminate feeling is superior. Wholesome and unwholesome feeling is inferior; indeterminate feeling is superior.
Painful feeling is inferior; pleasant feeling and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling are superior.
Pleasant and painful feelings are inferior; neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is superior.
Feeling of one who has not attained meditative absorption is inferior; feeling of one who has attained meditative absorption is superior.
Feeling associated with taints is inferior; feeling dissociated from taints is sublime.
Furthermore, feeling should be regarded as inferior or sublime in relation to this or that specific feeling.
In this context, what is feeling that is distant?
Unwholesome feeling is distant from wholesome and indeterminate feelings;
wholesome and indeterminate feelings are distant from unwholesome feeling; wholesome feeling is distant from unwholesome and indeterminate feelings.
Unwholesome and indeterminate feelings are distant from wholesome feeling;
indeterminate feelings are distant from wholesome and unwholesome feelings;
wholesome and unwholesome feelings are distant from indeterminate feeling.
Painful feeling is distant from pleasant feeling and from neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling;
pleasant feeling and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling are distant from painful feeling;
pleasant feeling is distant from painful feeling and from neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
Painful feeling and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling are distant from pleasant feeling;
neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is distant from painful and pleasant feelings;
painful and pleasant feelings are distant from neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
The feeling of one who has not attained meditative absorption is distant from the feeling of one who has attained it;
the feeling of one who has attained it is distant from the feeling of one who has not attained it.
Feeling accompanied by taints is distant from feeling free from taints.
Taintless feeling is distant from tainted feeling—
this is called feeling that is distant.
In this context, what is feeling that is near?
Unwholesome feeling is proximate to unwholesome feeling;
wholesome feeling is proximate to wholesome feeling;
indeterminate feeling is proximate to indeterminate feeling.
Painful feeling is proximate to painful feeling;
pleasant feeling is proximate to pleasant feeling;
neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is proximate to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.

The feeling of one who has not attained meditative absorption is proximate to the feeling of one who has not attained meditative absorption; the feeling of one who has attained meditative absorption is proximate to the feeling of one who has attained meditative absorption.
Feeling accompanied by taints is proximate to feeling accompanied by taints.
Taintless feeling is proximate to taintless feeling.
This is called proximate feeling.
Furthermore, depending on this or that particular feeling, feelings are to be regarded as either distant or proximate.
1.3. The Aggregate of Perception (Saññākkhandha).
Therein, what is the aggregate of perception?

Whatever perception there is—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—all that, having gathered it together as one and condensed it—[is called the aggregate of perception].
This is called the aggregate of perception (*saññā-khandha*).
In this context, what is past perception?
That perception which is past, ceased, vanished, changed, come to an end, utterly passed away, and having arisen, has disappeared.
The past is comprised by the past: perception born of eye-contact, perception born of ear-contact,
perception born of nose-contact, perception born of tongue-contact, perception born of body-contact, and perception born of mind-contact—
this is called past perception.
In this context, what is perception that has not yet come to be?
It is that perception which is unborn, unbecome, unarisen, unproduced, not fully produced, not manifested, unarisen,
not fully arisen, not established, not fully established, future, and comprised within the future— namely, perception born of eye-contact and perception born of ear-contact.
Perception born of nose-contact, perception born of tongue-contact, perception born of body-contact, and perception born of mind-contact—
this is called future perception.
In this context, what is present perception?
Whatever perception has been born, become, produced, brought forth, manifested, arisen, fully arisen, emerged,
fully emerged, present, and included within the present moment— namely, perception born of eye-contact,
perception born of ear-contact, perception born of nose-contact, perception born of tongue-contact, perception born of body-contact, and perception born of mind-contact.
This is called present perception.
In this context, what is internal perception?
It is that perception which, for various beings, is internal, individual, personal, and grasped.
Perception born of eye-contact, perception born of ear-contact, perception born of nose-contact, perception born of tongue-contact,
perception born of body-contact, and perception born of mind-contact—
this is called internal perception.
In this context, what is perception external?
It is that perception which, for various other beings and other persons, is internal, personal, one's own,
individual, and acquired— perception born of eye-contact, perception born of ear-contact, perception born of nose-contact, and perception born of tongue-contact.
Perception born of body-contact and perception born of mind-contact—
this is called external perception.
In this context, what is gross perception and what is subtle perception?
Perception born of contact through resistance is gross; perception born of contact through designation is subtle.
Unwholesome perception is gross; wholesome and indeterminate perception is subtle. Wholesome and unwholesome perception is gross; indeterminate perception is subtle.
Perception associated with painful feeling is gross; perception associated with pleasant and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings is subtle.
Perception associated with pleasant and painful feelings is gross; perception associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is subtle.
Perception of one who has not attained meditative absorption is gross; perception of one who has attained meditative absorption is subtle.
Perception accompanied by taints is gross; perception free from taints is subtle.
Furthermore, depending upon this or that perception, perceptions are to be regarded as gross or subtle.
In this context, what is perception that is inferior and what is perception that is superior?
Unwholesome perception is inferior; wholesome and indeterminate perception is superior. Wholesome and unwholesome perception is inferior; indeterminate perception is superior.
Perception associated with painful feeling is inferior; perception associated with pleasant and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings is superior.
Perception associated with pleasant and painful feelings is inferior; perception associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is superior.
Perception of one who has not attained meditative absorption is inferior; perception of one who has attained absorption is superior.
Perception accompanied by taints is inferior; perception free from taints is superior.
Furthermore, by depending on this or that perception, perceptions are to be seen as inferior or superior.
In this context, what perception is distant?
Unwholesome perception is distant from wholesome and indeterminate perceptions.
Wholesome and indeterminate perception is distant from unwholesome perception; wholesome perception is distant from unwholesome and indeterminate perceptions;
unwholesome and indeterminate perception is distant from wholesome perception.
Indeterminate perception is distant from wholesome and unwholesome perceptions;
wholesome and unwholesome perceptions are distant from indeterminate perception.
Perception associated with painful feeling is distant from perceptions associated with pleasant and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings.
Perception associated with pleasant and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings is distant from perception associated with painful feeling;
perception associated with pleasant feeling is distant from perceptions associated with painful and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings;
and perception associated with painful and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings is distant from perception associated with pleasant feeling.
Perception associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is distant from perceptions associated with pleasant or painful feelings;
perceptions associated with pleasant or painful feelings are distant from perception associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
Perception of one who has not attained meditative absorption is distant from the perception of one who has attained absorption.
The perception of one who has attained meditative absorption is distant from the perception of one who has not attained it.
Contaminated perception is distant from uncontaminated perception;
uncontaminated perception is distant from contaminated perception.
This is called perception that is distant.
In this context, what is perception that is near?
Unwholesome perception is near to unwholesome perception.
Wholesome perception is proximate to wholesome perception;
indeterminate perception is proximate to indeterminate perception.
Perception associated with painful feeling is proximate to perception associated with painful feeling.
Perception associated with pleasant feeling is proximate to perception associated with pleasant feeling;
perception associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is proximate to perception associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling;
the perception of one who has not attained meditative absorption is proximate to the perception of one who has not attained meditative absorption.
The perception of one who has attained meditative absorption is proximate to the perception of one who has attained meditative absorption.
Tainted perception is proximate to tainted perception;
untainted perception is proximate to untainted perception.
This is called proximate perception.
Or rather, depending on this or that perception, perceptions should be regarded as distant or proximate.
1.4. The Aggregate of Volitional Formations (Saṅkhārakkhandha)
In this context, what is the aggregate of volitional formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*)?

Whatever volitional formations there are—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—all these, having been gathered together and condensed into one, are called the aggregate of volitional formations.
In this context, what are past volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*)?
Those volitional formations that are past, ceased, vanished, changed, come to an end, utterly passed away, which, having arisen, have vanished;
which are past and included within the past—namely, volition born of eye-contact and volition born of ear-contact.
Volition born of nose-contact, volition born of tongue-contact, volition born of body-contact, and volition born of mind-contact—
these are called past formations (*saṅkhāra*).
In this context, which are the future formations?
Those formations that are unborn, unbecome, unoriginated, unproduced, unmanifested, unarisen, not fully arisen, not established,
not fully established, future, and comprised within the future: namely, volition born of eye-contact, volition born of ear-contact, volition born of nose-contact,
volition born of tongue-contact, volition born of body-contact, and volition born of mind-contact.
These are called future formations.
In this context, what are present formations?
Those formations which have been born, become, fully arisen, produced, fully manifested, appeared, arisen, and fully arisen.
Arising, fully arisen, present, and included within the present category:
volition born of eye-contact, volition born of ear-contact, volition born of nose-contact, volition born of tongue-contact, volition born of body-contact,
and volition born of mind-contact.
These are called present formations (*saṅkhārā*).
Therein, what are internal formations?
Those formations which, for this or that being, are internal, personal, one's own, individual, and clung-to (*upādinnā*).
Volition born of eye-contact, volition born of ear-contact, volition born of nose-contact, volition born of tongue-contact,
volition born of body-contact, and volition born of mind-contact—
these are called internal formations.
In this context, what are volitional formations that are external?
Those volitional formations which, for various other beings and other persons, are internal, personal, one's own, individual, and clung-to:
namely, volition born of eye-contact, volition born of ear-contact, and volition born of nose-contact.
Volition born of tongue-contact, volition born of body-contact, and volition born of mind-contact—
these are called external formations (*saṅkhāra*).
In this context, which formations are gross and which are subtle?
Unwholesome formations are gross; wholesome and indeterminate formations are subtle. Wholesome and unwholesome formations are gross; indeterminate formations are subtle.
Formations associated with painful feeling are gross; formations associated with pleasant and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings are subtle.
Volitional formations associated with pleasant and painful feelings are gross; volitional formations associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling are subtle.
Volitional formations of one who has not attained meditative absorption are gross; volitional formations of one who has attained meditative absorption are subtle.
Volitional formations subject to taints are gross; volitional formations free from taints are subtle.
Furthermore, those formations should be regarded as gross or subtle in relation to one another.
In this context, which formations are inferior and which are superior?
Unwholesome formations are inferior; wholesome and indeterminate formations are superior.
Wholesome and unwholesome formations are inferior; indeterminate formations are superior.
Formations associated with painful feeling are inferior; formations associated with pleasant and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings are superior.
Formations associated with pleasant and painful feelings are inferior; formations associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling are superior.
The formations of one who has not attained meditative absorption are inferior; the formations of one who has attained are superior.
Formations associated with the taints are inferior; formations free from the taints are superior.
Furthermore, formations should be regarded as inferior or superior depending on the specific formations they are based upon.
In this context, which formations are distant?
Unwholesome formations are distant from wholesome and indeterminate formations;
wholesome and indeterminate formations are distant from unwholesome formations.
Wholesome formations are distant from unwholesome and indeterminate formations;
unwholesome and indeterminate formations are distant from wholesome formations;
indeterminate formations are distant from wholesome and unwholesome formations.
Wholesome and unwholesome formations are distant from indeterminate formations.
Formations associated with painful feeling are distant from formations associated with pleasant and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings;
formations associated with pleasant and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings are distant from formations associated with painful feeling.
Volitional formations associated with pleasant feeling are distant from volitional formations associated with painful and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings;
volitional formations associated with painful and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings are distant from volitional formations associated with pleasant feeling;
volitional formations associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling are distant from volitional formations associated with pleasant and painful feelings.
Volitional formations associated with pleasant and painful feelings are distant from volitional formations associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
The volitional formations of one who has not attained meditative absorption are distant from the volitional formations of one who has attained absorption;
the volitional formations of one who has attained absorption are distant from the volitional formations of one who has not attained absorption.
Conditioned phenomena associated with the taints are distant from conditioned phenomena free from the taints;
conditioned phenomena free from the taints are distant from conditioned phenomena associated with the taints.
These are called "distant conditioned phenomena."
In this context, which formations are proximate?
Unwholesome formations are proximate to unwholesome formations;
wholesome formations are proximate to wholesome formations.
Indeterminate formations are proximate to indeterminate formations.
Formations associated with painful feeling are proximate to formations associated with painful feeling;
formations associated with pleasant feeling are proximate to formations associated with pleasant feeling.
Volitional formations associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling are proximate to volitional formations associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.

Volitional formations of one who has not attained meditative absorption are proximate to the volitional formations of one who has not attained meditative absorption; volitional formations of one who has attained meditative absorption are proximate to the volitional formations of one who has attained meditative absorption.
Conditioned phenomena associated with taints are proximate to conditioned phenomena associated with taints;
unconditioned phenomena are proximate to unconditioned phenomena.
These are called proximate conditioned phenomena.
Or else, those formations themselves, taken one by one, should be seen as formations that are distant or near.
1.5. The Aggregate of Consciousness:
Therein, what is the aggregate of consciousness?

Whatever consciousness there is—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—all that, having gathered it together as one and condensed it—this is called the aggregate of consciousness (*viññāṇakkhandha*).
In this context, what is past consciousness?
That consciousness which is past, ceased, vanished, changed, come to an end, utterly passed away, having arisen and then vanished,
past, and included within the past— namely, eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness,
tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness.
This is called past consciousness.
In this context, what is future consciousness?
That consciousness which is unborn, has not come to be, has not been produced, is unarisen, has not manifested, and has not appeared.
That which has not arisen, has not been undertaken, has not emerged, is future, and is comprised within the future:
eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness—
this is called future consciousness.
In this context, what is present consciousness?
That consciousness which is born, become, fully arisen, produced, fully produced, manifested, arisen, fully arisen, emerged, fully emerged, present,
and included within the category of the present— namely, eye-consciousness and ear-consciousness.
Olfactory consciousness, gustatory consciousness, tactile consciousness, and mental consciousness—
this is called present consciousness.
In this context, what is internal consciousness?
Whatever consciousness is internal, belonging to oneself, individual, personal, and clung-to— eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness,
and mind-consciousness— this is called internal consciousness.
In this context, what is external consciousness?
Whatever consciousness there is— internal, personal, one's own, individual, and clung-to— of various other beings and other persons,
namely: eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness,
tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness.
This is called consciousness that is external.
In this context, what is gross consciousness and what is subtle consciousness?
Unwholesome consciousness is gross; wholesome and indeterminate consciousnesses are subtle.
Wholesome and unwholesome consciousnesses are gross; indeterminate consciousness is subtle.
Consciousness associated with painful feeling is gross; consciousnesses associated with pleasant and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings are subtle.
Consciousnesses associated with pleasant and painful feelings are gross; consciousness associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is subtle.
The consciousness of one who has not attained meditative absorption is gross; the consciousness of one who has attained is subtle.
Consciousness associated with taints is gross; consciousness free from taints is subtle.
Furthermore, depending on this or that specific consciousness, consciousness should be regarded as either gross or subtle.
In this context, what is consciousness that is inferior and what is consciousness that is superior?
Unwholesome consciousness is inferior; wholesome and indeterminate consciousnesses are superior. Wholesome and unwholesome consciousnesses are inferior; indeterminate consciousness is superior.
Consciousness associated with painful feeling is inferior; consciousnesses associated with pleasant feeling and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling are superior.
Consciousnesses associated with pleasant and painful feelings are inferior; consciousness associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is superior.
Consciousness of one who has not attained meditative absorption is inferior; consciousness of one who has attained meditative absorption is superior.
Consciousness with taints is inferior; consciousness without taints is superior.
Furthermore, depending on this or that specific consciousness, consciousness is to be seen as either inferior or superior.
In this context, what is consciousness that is distant?
Unwholesome consciousness is distant from wholesome and indeterminate consciousnesses;
wholesome and indeterminate consciousnesses are distant from unwholesome consciousnesses; wholesome consciousness is distant from unwholesome and indeterminate consciousnesses.
Unwholesome and indeterminate consciousnesses are distant from wholesome consciousnesses;
indeterminate consciousness is distant from wholesome and unwholesome consciousnesses;
wholesome and unwholesome consciousnesses are distant from indeterminate consciousnesses.
Consciousness associated with painful feeling is distant from consciousnesses associated with pleasant and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings;
consciousnesses associated with pleasant and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings are distant from consciousness associated with painful feeling;
consciousness associated with pleasant feeling is distant from consciousnesses associated with painful and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings.
Consciousnesses associated with painful and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings are distant from consciousness associated with pleasant feeling;
consciousness associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is distant from consciousnesses associated with pleasant and painful feelings;
consciousnesses associated with pleasant and painful feelings are distant from consciousness associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
The consciousness of one who has not attained is distant from the consciousness of one who has attained;
the consciousness of one who has attained is distant from the consciousness of one who has not attained.
Consciousness with taints is distant from consciousness without taints.
Taintless consciousness is distant from tainted consciousnesses—
this is called consciousness that is distant.
In this context, what is consciousness that is near?
Unwholesome consciousness is proximate to unwholesome consciousness;
wholesome consciousness is proximate to wholesome consciousness;
indeterminate consciousness is proximate to indeterminate consciousness.
Consciousness associated with painful feeling is proximate to consciousness associated with painful feeling;
consciousness associated with pleasant feeling is proximate to consciousness associated with pleasant feeling;
consciousness associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is proximate to consciousness associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
The consciousness of one who has not attained is near to the consciousness of one who has not attained;
the consciousness of one who has attained is near to the consciousness of one who has attained.
Consciousness accompanied by taints is near to consciousness accompanied by taints.
Taintless consciousness is proximate to taintless consciousness—
this is called consciousness that is proximate.
Furthermore, depending on this or that consciousness, consciousness should be regarded as distant or proximate.
The Exposition of the Discourses (Suttantabhājanīya). 2.
The Exposition of the Abhidhamma (Abhidhammabhājanīya):
The five aggregates (pañcakkhandhā)—
The aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations, and the aggregate of consciousness.
2.1. The Aggregate of Form:
Therein, what is the aggregate of form?
The aggregate of form is of one kind:
all form is not a cause, is rootless, is dissociated from roots, is conditioned, is formed, is mundane,
is with taints, is subject to fetters, is subject to ties, is subject to floods, is subject to yokes, is subject to hindrances, and is adhered to.
It is subject to clinging, defiled, indeterminate, without an object, non-mental, dissociated from consciousness, neither resultant nor producing resultant states, undefiled yet defiled,
neither with applied thought and sustained thought, nor without applied thought and with sustained thought only, without applied thought and without sustained thought, neither accompanied by rapture,
nor accompanied by pleasure, nor accompanied by equanimity, and is neither to be abandoned by vision nor by cultivation.
It is to be abandoned; its cause is neither to be abandoned by vision nor by cultivation; it neither leads to accumulation nor to diminution;
it is neither for those in training nor for those beyond training; it is limited, belonging to the sense sphere, not the fine-material sphere, nor the immaterial sphere;

it is included within the mundane, not the supramundane; it is undetermined, not leading to escape; it has arisen; it is cognizable by the six consciousnesses; it is impermanent and overcome by aging.
Thus is the aggregate of form by way of onefold division. By way of twofold division, the aggregate of form is as follows:
there is form that is derived, and there is form that is not derived.
There is form that is clung-to; there is form that is not clung-to. There is form that is both clung-to and conducive to clinging; there is form that is neither clung-to nor conducive to clinging.
There is form that is visible; there is form that is invisible.
There is matter that is with resistance; there is matter that is without resistance.
There is matter that is a faculty; there is matter that is not a faculty.
There is matter that is a great primary element; there is matter that is not a great primary element.
There is matter that is intimation; there is matter that is not intimation.
There is matter originated by mind; there is matter not originated by mind.
There is matter coexistent with mind; there is matter not coexistent with mind.
There is form that accompanies the mind; there is form that does not accompany the mind.
There is internal form; there is external form.
There is gross form; there is subtle form.
There is form that is distant; there is form that is near ... [and so on] ... there is form that is edible food; there is form that is not edible food.
Thus is the aggregate of form twofold.
(It should be analyzed here in the same way as it was analyzed in the *Rūpakanda*.)
The aggregate of form is threefold:
that form which is internal is derived; that form which is external is either derived or non-derived.
That form which is internal is clung-to; that form which is external is either clung-to or not clung-to.
That form which is internal is acquired and subject to clinging; that form which is external is either acquired and subject to clinging, or not acquired but subject to clinging...
That form which is internal is not edible food; that form which is external is either edible food or not edible food.
Thus is the aggregate of form threefold.
The aggregate of form is fourfold:
that form which is derived is either clung-to or not clung-to;
that form which is non-derived is either clung-to or not clung-to.
Of that form which is derived, some is acquired and subject to clinging, and some is not acquired but subject to clinging.
Of that form which is not derived, some is acquired and subject to clinging, and some is not acquired but subject to clinging.
Of that form which is derived, some is with resistance, and some is without resistance.
Of that form which is not derived, some is with resistance and some is without resistance.
Of that form which is derived, some is gross and some is subtle;
of that form which is not derived, some is gross and some is subtle.
That form which is derived exists far away, exists near;
that form which is not derived exists far away, exists near ... [and so on] ...
form that is seen, heard, sensed, and cognized.
Thus is the aggregate of form by way of fourfold division.
The aggregate of form by way of fivefold division is:
the earth element, the water element, the fire element, the air element, and that form which is derived.
Thus is the aggregate of form by way of fivefold division.
The aggregate of form by way of sixfold division:
form cognizable by the eye, form cognizable by the ear, form cognizable by the nose, form cognizable by the tongue, form cognizable by the body, and form cognizable by the mind.
Thus is the aggregate of form by way of sixfold division.
The aggregate of form by way of sevenfold division is:

form cognizable by the eye, form cognizable by the ear, form cognizable by the nose, form cognizable by the tongue, form cognizable by the body, form cognizable by the mind-element, and form cognizable by the mind-consciousness-element.
Thus is the aggregate of form by way of sevenfold division.
The aggregate of form by way of eightfold division:
form cognizable by the eye, form cognizable by the ear, form cognizable by the nose, form cognizable by the tongue...
There is form cognizable by the body; there is form that is pleasant to touch, and there is form that is painful to touch;
there is form cognizable by the mind-element, and there is form cognizable by the mind-consciousness-element.
Thus is the aggregate of form eightfold.
The aggregate of form is ninefold:
the eye faculty, the ear faculty, the nose faculty, the tongue faculty, the body faculty, the female faculty, the male faculty, the life faculty, and that form which is not a faculty.
Thus is the aggregate of form ninefold.
The aggregate of form is tenfold:

the eye faculty, the ear faculty, the nose faculty, the tongue faculty, the body faculty, the female faculty, the male faculty, the life faculty, form that is not a faculty and is impinging, and form that is not impinging.
Thus is the aggregate of form tenfold.
The aggregate of form is of eleven kinds:
the eye base, the ear base, the nose base, the tongue base, the body base, the visible-form base,
the sound base, the odor base, the flavor base, the tangible-object base, and that form which is non-demonstrable and non-reactive.
Included in the sphere of mental phenomena (*dhammāyatana*).
Thus is the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*) in its elevenfold aspect.
This is called the aggregate of form.
2.2. The Aggregate of Feeling (Vedanākkhandha).
Therein, what is the aggregate of feeling?
The aggregate of feeling is of one kind: [namely, by way of the six bases].
Associated with contact.
The aggregate of feeling is twofold:
there is that which is with root-cause, and there is that which is without root-cause.
The aggregate of feeling is threefold:
there is the wholesome, there is the unwholesome, and there is the indeterminate.
The aggregate of feeling is fourfold:

There is that which belongs to the sense sphere, there is that which belongs to the fine-material sphere, there is that which belongs to the immaterial sphere, and there is that which is not included [within the spheres].
The aggregate of feeling is fivefold:
there is the faculty of pleasure, there is the faculty of pain, there is the faculty of mental joy, there is the faculty of mental grief, and there is the faculty of equanimity.
Thus is the aggregate of feeling fivefold.
The aggregate of feeling is sixfold:
feeling born of eye-contact, feeling born of ear-contact, feeling born of nose-contact, feeling born of tongue-contact, feeling born of body-contact, and feeling born of mind-contact.
Thus is the aggregate of feeling sixfold.
The aggregate of feeling is sevenfold:
feeling born of eye-contact, feeling born of ear-contact, feeling born of nose-contact, feeling born of tongue-contact...
Feeling, feeling born of body-contact, feeling born of mind-element-contact, and feeling born of mind-consciousness-element-contact.
Thus is the aggregate of feeling by way of sevenfold division.
By way of eightfold division, the aggregate of feeling is as follows:
There is feeling born of eye-contact, feeling born of ear-contact, feeling born of nose-contact, feeling born of tongue-contact,
feeling born of body-contact— there is pleasant [feeling] and there is painful [feeling];
and there is feeling born of mind-element contact and feeling born of mind-consciousness-element contact.
Thus is the aggregate of feeling by way of eightfold division.
The aggregate of feeling by way of ninefold division:
feeling born of eye-contact, feeling born of ear-contact, feeling born of nose-contact, feeling born of tongue-contact...
Feeling, feeling born of body-contact, feeling born of mind-element-contact, and feeling born of mind-consciousness-element-contact:
there is that which is wholesome, there is that which is unwholesome, and there is that which is indeterminate.
Thus is the aggregate of feeling ninefold.
The aggregate of feeling is tenfold:
feeling born of eye-contact, feeling born of ear-contact, feeling born of nose-contact, feeling born of tongue-contact,
feeling born of body-contact— which is either pleasant or painful— and feeling born of mind-element-contact.
Feeling born of contact with the mind-consciousness element is wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
Thus is the aggregate of feeling by way of tenfold division.
The aggregate of feeling by way of singlefold division:
Associated with contact.
The aggregate of feeling is twofold:
there is that which is with root-cause, and there is that which is without root-cause.
The aggregate of feeling is threefold:
there is that which is kamma-result, there is that which is of a nature to produce kamma-result, and there is that which is neither kamma-result nor of a nature to produce kamma-result.
There is that which is grasped and subject to clinging, there is that which is not grasped but subject to clinging, and there is that which is neither grasped nor subject to clinging.
There is that which is defiled and subject to defilement; there is that which is undefiled but subject to defilement;

there is that which is neither defiled nor subject to defilement. There is that which is accompanied by applied thought and sustained thought; there is that which is without applied thought but with sustained thought only; there is that which is without applied thought and without sustained thought.
There is that which is to be abandoned by vision; there is that which is to be abandoned by cultivation; there is that which is to be abandoned neither by vision nor by cultivation.

There is that which has a root to be abandoned by vision; there is that which has a root to be abandoned by cultivation; there is that which has a root to be abandoned neither by vision nor by cultivation.
There is that which leads to accumulation; there is that which leads to diminution; there is that which leads neither to accumulation nor to diminution.
There is that which pertains to the trainee; there is that which pertains to the one beyond training; there is that which pertains neither to the trainee nor to the one beyond training.
There is the limited, there is the exalted, and there is the immeasurable.
There is that which has a limited object, there is that which has an exalted object, and there is that which has an immeasurable object.
There is the inferior, there is the intermediate, and there is the superior.
There is that which is fixed in falsehood; there is that which is fixed in rightness; there is that which is unfixed.
There is that which has the Path as its object; there is that which has the Path as its cause; there is that which has the Path as its predominance.
There is that which has arisen; there is that which has not yet arisen; there is that which is subject to arising.
There is the past, there is the future, there is the present.
There is that which has the past as its object, there is that which has the future as its object, there is that which has the present as its object.
There is the internal, there is the external, there is the internal-external.
There is that with internal object, there is that with external object, there is that with both internal and external object ... [and so on] ...
Thus is the aggregate of feeling by way of tenfold division.
The aggregate of feeling by way of singlefold division:
Associated with contact.
The aggregate of feeling is twofold:

there is that associated with a root, and there is that dissociated from a root ... [and so on] ... there is that which is neither a root nor has a root, and there is that which is neither a root nor does not have a root.
There is that which is mundane; there is that which is supramundane.
There is that which is cognizable by someone; there is that which is not cognizable by anyone.
There is that which is with taints; there is that which is without taints.

There is that which is associated with the taints; there is that which is dissociated from the taints. There is that which is dissociated from the taints yet subject to them; there is that which is dissociated from the taints and not subject to them.
There is that which is conducive to fetters; there is that which is not conducive to fetters.
There is that which is associated with the fetters; there is that which is dissociated from the fetters.
There is that which is dissociated from the fetters but is subject to the fetters; there is that which is dissociated from the fetters and is not subject to the fetters.
There is that which is conducive to the knots; there is that which is not conducive to the knots.
There is that which is associated with the fetters; there is that which is dissociated from the fetters.

There is that which is dissociated from the fetters but conducive to the fetters; there is that which is dissociated from the fetters and not conducive to the fetters. There is that which is conducive to the floods; there is that which is not conducive to the floods.

There is that which is associated with the floods; there is that which is dissociated from the floods. There is that which is dissociated from the floods but is subject to the floods; there is that which is dissociated from the floods and not subject to the floods. There is that which is subject to the yokes;
there is that which is not subject to the yokes.
There is that which is associated with the yokes; there is that which is dissociated from the yokes.
There is that which is dissociated from the yokes but bound by the yokes; there is that which is dissociated from the yokes and not bound by the yokes.
There is that which is subject to the hindrances; there is that which is not subject to the hindrances.
There is that which is associated with the hindrances; there is that which is dissociated from the hindrances.
There is that which is dissociated from the hindrances yet subject to them; there is that which is dissociated from the hindrances and not subject to them.
There is that which is misapprehended; there is that which is not misapprehended.

There is that which is associated with clinging; there is that which is dissociated from clinging. There is that which is dissociated from clinging but clung to; there is that which is dissociated from clinging and not clung to. There is that which is grasped; there is that which is not grasped.

There is that which is subject to clinging; there is that which is not subject to clinging. There is that which is associated with clinging; there is that which is dissociated from clinging. There is that which is dissociated from clinging yet subject to clinging; there is that which is dissociated from clinging and not subject to clinging.
There is that which is subject to defilement; there is that which is not subject to defilement.
There is that which is defiled; there is that which is undefiled.
There is that which is associated with defilement; there is that which is dissociated from defilement.
There is that which is dissociated from the defilements yet subject to defilement; there is that which is dissociated from the defilements and not subject to defilement.
There is that which is to be abandoned by seeing; there is that which is not to be abandoned by seeing.
There is that which is to be abandoned by cultivation; there is that which is not to be abandoned by cultivation.
There is that which has a root to be abandoned by vision; there is that which does not have a root to be abandoned by vision.
There is that which has a root to be abandoned by cultivation; there is that which does not have a root to be abandoned by cultivation.
There is that which is accompanied by applied thought; there is that which is without applied thought.
There is that with investigation, there is that without investigation.
There is that accompanied by rapture, there is that without rapture. There is that associated with rapture, there is that not associated with rapture.
There is that which belongs to the sense sphere; there is that which does not belong to the sense sphere.
There is that which belongs to the fine-material sphere; there is that which does not belong to the fine-material sphere.
There is that which belongs to the immaterial sphere; there is that which does not belong to the immaterial sphere.
There is that which is included, and there is that which is not included.
There is that which leads to liberation, and there is that which does not lead to liberation.
There is that which is fixed, and there is that which is not fixed.
There is that which has an equal above it, and there is that which has nothing above it.
There is that which is with conflict, and there is that which is without conflict.
The aggregate of feeling is threefold:
There is wholesome, there is unwholesome, there is indeterminate … [and so on] … Thus is the aggregate of feeling by way of tenfold division.
The aggregate of feeling by way of a singlefold division: [is wholesome].
Associated with contact.
The aggregate of feeling is twofold:
there is that which is with conflict, and there is that which is without conflict.
The aggregate of feeling is threefold:
there is that which is kamma-result, there is that which is of a nature to produce kamma-result, and there is that which is neither kamma-result nor of a nature to produce kamma-result.

There is that which is grasped and favourable to grasping ... [and so on] ... there is that which has an internal object, there is that which has an external object, and there is that which has both an internal and external object ... [and so on].
Thus is the aggregate of feeling by way of tenfold classification.
[End of] the section based on pairs.
The aggregate of feeling by way of singlefold classification:
Associated with contact.
The aggregate of feeling is twofold:
there is that which is with root-cause, and there is that which is without root-cause.
The aggregate of feeling is threefold:
there is wholesome, there is unwholesome, and there is indeterminate … [as before] … Thus is the aggregate of feeling tenfold.
The aggregate of feeling is of one kind:
associated with contact.
The aggregate of feeling is of two kinds:
There is that which is associated with a root; there is that which is dissociated from a root.
The aggregate of feeling is threefold:
there is the wholesome, there is the unwholesome, and there is the indeterminate ... [and so forth] ...
Thus is the aggregate of feeling by way of tenfold classification.
The aggregate of feeling by way of singlefold classification:
associated with contact.
The aggregate of feeling is twofold:
there is that which is not-rooted but with-root, and there is that which is neither-rooted nor without-root.
There is that which is mundane, and there is that which is supramundane.
There is that which is cognizable by someone; there is that which is not cognizable by anyone.
There is that which is with taints; there is that which is without taints. There is that which is associated with taints; there is that which is dissociated from taints.
There is that which is dissociated from the taints yet accompanied by taints; there is that which is dissociated from the taints and free from taints ... [and so on] ... There is that with conflict;
there is that without conflict. The aggregate of feeling is threefold:
there is the wholesome, there is the unwholesome, and there is the indeterminate ... [and so on].
Thus is the aggregate of feeling by way of tenfold classification.
The aggregate of feeling by way of a singlefold classification:
associated with contact.
The aggregate of feeling is twofold:
there is that which is with root-cause, and there is that which is without root-cause.
The aggregate of feeling is threefold:
There is that which is result; there is that which has the nature of being a result; there is that which is neither result nor having the nature of being a result.
There is that which is acquired and subject to clinging; there is that which is not acquired but subject to clinging; there is that which is neither acquired nor subject to clinging.
There is that which is defiled and subject to defilement; there is that which is undefiled but subject to defilement; there is that which is neither defiled nor subject to defilement.
There is that with applied thought and sustained thought; there is that without applied thought and with sustained thought only; there is that without applied thought and without sustained thought.
There is that to be abandoned by seeing; there is that to be abandoned by cultivation; there is that to be abandoned neither by seeing nor by cultivation.
There is that whose root is to be abandoned by seeing; there is that whose root is to be abandoned by cultivation; there is that whose root is to be abandoned neither by seeing nor by cultivation.
There is that which leads to accumulation; there is that which leads to diminution; there is that which leads neither to accumulation nor to diminution.
There is that which pertains to the trainee; there is that which pertains to the one beyond training; there is that which pertains neither to the trainee nor to the one beyond training.
There is the limited; there is the exalted; there is the immeasurable.
There is that which has a limited object, there is that which has a sublime object, and there is that which has an immeasurable object.
There is that which is inferior, there is that which is intermediate, and there is that which is superior.
There is that which is fixed in the wrong way, there is that which is fixed in the right way, and there is that which is unfixed.
There is that which has the Path as its object; there is that which has the Path as its cause; there is that which has the Path as its predominance.
There is that which is arisen; there is that which is unarisen; there is that which is subject to arising.
There is that which is past; there is that which is future; there is that which is present.
There is that which has a past object, there is that which has a future object, and there is that which has a present object.
There is that which is internal, there is that which is external, and there is that which is both internal and external.
There is that which has an internal object, there is that which has an external object, and there is that which has an internal-external object ... [and so on].
Thus is the aggregate of feeling by way of tenfold division.
The aggregate of feeling by way of singlefold division:
associated with contact.
The aggregate of feeling is twofold:
there is that associated with a root-cause, and there is that dissociated from a root-cause.
There is that which is neither a root-cause nor has a root-cause, and there is that which is neither a root-cause nor does not have a root-cause.
There is that which is mundane; there is that which is supramundane.
There is that which is cognizable by someone; there is that which is not cognizable by anyone.
There is that which is with taints; there is that which is without taints.
There is that which is associated with the taints; there is that which is dissociated from the taints.
There is that which is dissociated from the taints yet accompanied by taints; there is that which is dissociated from the taints and free from taints.
There is that which is conducive to fetters; there is that which is not conducive to fetters ... [and so on] ... there is that which is with conflict; there is that which is without conflict.
The aggregate of feeling is threefold:
there is that with an internal object, there is that with an external object, and there is that with both an internal and external object...
[and so on] ... Thus is the aggregate of feeling tenfold.
The triad based on three factors.
By way of a single mode, the aggregate of feeling is associated with contact.
The aggregate of feeling is twofold:
there is that which is with root-cause, and there is that which is without root-cause.
The aggregate of feeling is threefold:
There is the wholesome, there is the unwholesome, there is the indeterminate ... [and so on] ...
Thus is the aggregate of feeling by way of tenfold division.
The aggregate of feeling by way of a singlefold division:
Associated with contact.
The aggregate of feeling is twofold:
there is that associated with a root, and there is that dissociated from a root.
The aggregate of feeling is threefold:
there is that which is kamma-result, there is that which is of a nature to produce kamma-result, and there is that which is neither kamma-result nor of a nature to produce kamma-result...
Thus is the aggregate of feeling tenfold.
The aggregate of feeling is of one kind:
associated with contact.
The aggregate of feeling is of two kinds:
There is that which is neither caused nor accompanied by a cause; there is that which is neither caused nor uncaused.
The aggregate of feeling is threefold:
there is that which is clung-to and subject to clinging; there is that which is not clung-to but subject to clinging; there is that which is neither clung-to nor subject to clinging ... [and so on].
Thus is the aggregate of feeling by way of tenfold classification.
The aggregate of feeling by way of singlefold classification:
associated with contact.
The aggregate of feeling is twofold:
there is the mundane, and there is the supramundane.
The aggregate of feeling is threefold:
There is that which is defiled and subject to defilement; there is that which is undefiled but subject to defilement; there is that which is undefiled and not subject to defilement...
[and so on]. Thus is the aggregate of feeling by way of tenfold division.
The aggregate of feeling by way of a singlefold division:
Associated with contact.
The aggregate of feeling is twofold:
there is that which is cognizable by something, and there is that which is not cognizable by anything.
The aggregate of feeling is threefold:

there is that accompanied by applied thought and sustained thought; there is that without applied thought and with sustained thought only; there is that without applied thought and without sustained thought...
[and so on]... Thus is the aggregate of feeling tenfold.
The aggregate of feeling is of one kind:
associated with contact.
The aggregate of feeling is of two kinds:
There is that which is associated with taints; there is that which is dissociated from taints.
The aggregate of feeling is threefold:

there is that which is to be abandoned by vision, there is that which is to be abandoned by cultivation, and there is that which is to be abandoned neither by vision nor by cultivation... [and so on].
Thus is the aggregate of feeling by way of tenfold classification.
The aggregate of feeling by way of singlefold classification:
associated with contact.
The aggregate of feeling is twofold:
there is that associated with the taints, and there is that dissociated from the taints.
The aggregate of feeling is threefold:

There is that which has a root to be abandoned by vision; there is that which has a root to be abandoned by cultivation; there is that which has a root to be abandoned neither by vision nor by cultivation ...
[and so on] ... Thus is the aggregate of feeling tenfold.
The aggregate of feeling is singlefold: [as a whole].
Associated with contact.
The aggregate of feeling is twofold:
there is that which is dissociated from the taints yet subject to taints, and there is that which is dissociated from the taints and free from taints.
The aggregate of feeling is threefold:
there is that which leads to accumulation, there is that which leads to diminution, and there is that which leads neither to accumulation nor to diminution ...
[and so on] ... Thus is the aggregate of feeling tenfold.
The aggregate of feeling is of one kind:
associated with contact.
The aggregate of feeling is of two kinds:
There is that which is conducive to fetters; there is that which is not conducive to fetters.
The aggregate of feeling is threefold:
there is that pertaining to the trainee, there is that pertaining to the one beyond training, and there is that pertaining to neither the trainee nor the one beyond training... [and so on].
Thus is the aggregate of feeling by way of tenfold division.
The aggregate of feeling by way of a singlefold division:
associated with contact.
The aggregate of feeling is twofold:
there is that associated with the fetters, and there is that dissociated from the fetters.
The aggregate of feeling is threefold:
There is the limited, there is the exalted, there is the immeasurable … [as above] … Thus is the aggregate of feeling by way of tenfold division.
The aggregate of feeling by way of a singlefold division:
Associated with contact.
The aggregate of feeling is twofold:
there is that which is dissociated from the fetters but is subject to them; and there is that which is dissociated from the fetters and is not subject to them.
The aggregate of feeling is threefold:
there is that which has a limited object, there is that which has a sublime object, and there is that which has an immeasurable object...
[and so on] ... Thus is the aggregate of feeling tenfold.
The aggregate of feeling is of one kind:
associated with contact.
The aggregate of feeling is of two kinds:
There is that which is subject to bondage; there is that which is not subject to bondage.
The aggregate of feeling is threefold:
there is the inferior, there is the middling, and there is the superior … [and so on] …
Thus is the aggregate of feeling by way of tenfold classification.
The aggregate of feeling by way of singlefold classification:
associated with contact.
The aggregate of feeling is twofold:
there is that which is associated with the fetters, and there is that which is dissociated from the fetters.
The aggregate of feeling is threefold:
There is that which is fixed in falsehood; there is that which is fixed in truth; there is that which is unfixed ...
[and so on] ... Thus is the aggregate of feeling by way of tenfold division.
The aggregate of feeling by way of singlefold division:
Associated with contact.
The aggregate of feeling is twofold:
there is that which is dissociated from the fetters but is subject to them, and there is that which is dissociated from the fetters and is not subject to them.
The aggregate of feeling is threefold:
there is that which has the Path as its object, there is that which has the Path as its cause, and there is that which has the Path as its predominance...
[and so on] ... Thus is the aggregate of feeling tenfold.
The aggregate of feeling is of one kind:
associated with contact.
The aggregate of feeling is of two kinds:
There is that which is subject to the floods, and there is that which is not subject to the floods.
The aggregate of feeling is threefold:
there is that which has arisen, there is that which has not yet arisen, and there is that which is bound to arise... [and so on].
Thus is the aggregate of feeling by way of tenfold classification.
The aggregate of feeling by way of singlefold classification:
associated with contact.
The aggregate of feeling is twofold:
there is that associated with the floods, and there is that dissociated from the floods.
The aggregate of feeling is threefold:
There is the past, there is the future, there is the present ... [as above] ...
Thus is the aggregate of feeling by way of tenfold division. The aggregate of feeling by way of singlefold division: [is as follows].
Associated with contact.
The aggregate of feeling is twofold:
there is that which is dissociated from the floods but is subject to the floods, and there is that which is dissociated from the floods and not subject to the floods.
The aggregate of feeling is threefold:
there is that which has the past as its object, there is that which has the future as its object, and there is that which has the present as its object...
[and so on] ... Thus is the aggregate of feeling tenfold.
The aggregate of feeling is of one kind:
associated with contact.
The aggregate of feeling is of two kinds:
There is that which is conducive to yoga; there is that which is not conducive to yoga.
The aggregate of feeling is threefold:
there is the internal, there is the external, and there is the internal-external ... [and so on].
Thus is the aggregate of feeling by way of tenfold classification.
The aggregate of feeling by way of singlefold classification:
associated with contact.
The aggregate of feeling is twofold:

there is that which is associated with the yokes, and there is that which is dissociated from the yokes. The aggregate of feeling is threefold: [it is associated with the yokes, dissociated from the yokes, and] neither-associated-nor-dissociated-from-the-yokes.
There is that which has an internal object, there is that which has an external object, and there is that which has both an internal and external object... [and so on]...
Thus is the aggregate of feeling by way of tenfold division.

The aggregate of feeling is sevenfold:

there is the wholesome, there is the unwholesome, there is the indeterminate, there is that pertaining to the sense sphere, there is that pertaining to the fine-material sphere, there is that pertaining to the immaterial sphere, and there is that which is not included [within the realms].
Thus is the aggregate of feeling sevenfold.
Furthermore, the aggregate of feeling is sevenfold:

there is that which is resultant … [and so on] … there is that which has an internal object, there is that which has an external object, there is that which has both an internal and external object, there is that which belongs to the sense sphere, there is that which belongs to the fine-material sphere, there is that which belongs to the immaterial sphere, and there is that which is unincluded.
Thus is the aggregate of feeling sevenfold.
The aggregate of feeling is of twenty-four kinds:
there is the aggregate of feeling conditioned by eye-contact, which is wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate;
there is the aggregate of feeling conditioned by ear-contact … [and so on].
The aggregate of feeling conditioned by nose-contact …pe… the aggregate of feeling conditioned by tongue-contact …pe… the aggregate of feeling conditioned by body-contact …pe…

it consists of feeling born of eye-contact, feeling born of ear-contact, feeling born of nose-contact, feeling born of tongue-contact, feeling born of body-contact, and feeling born of mind-contact.
Thus is the aggregate of feeling of twenty-four kinds.
Furthermore, the aggregate of feeling is of twenty-four kinds:

there is the aggregate of feeling conditioned by eye-contact that is kamma-resultant … [and so on] … there is that with an internal object, there is that with an external object, there is that with both an internal and external object;
[this includes] feeling born of eye-contact … up to … feeling born of mind-contact.
The aggregate of feeling conditioned by ear-contact …pe… the aggregate of feeling conditioned by nose-contact …pe… the aggregate of feeling conditioned by tongue-contact …pe…
